title: Leaf Temperature, Boundary Layers and Plant-Level VPD Context

content.overview: Air temperature and relative humidity describe the room, but the leaf surface can be warmer or cooler than the surrounding air. Radiation, airflow, transpiration, and leaf position affect this difference and therefore influence plant-atmosphere vapor-pressure interpretation.

vocabulary.definition: The temperature of leaf tissue, which may differ from the surrounding air.
A thin region of relatively still air next to a leaf surface that influences heat and vapor exchange.
Energy transferred to or from a leaf by radiation, affecting leaf temperature independently of air temperature.

sections.title: Leaf and air temperatures can diverge
sections.body: Light absorption, transpiration, and air movement can shift leaf temperature above or below room air. This is why plant-level VPD calculations should specify whether they use air temperature or measured leaf temperature.

sections.title: Airflow changes exchange
sections.body: Moving air reduces the thickness of the leaf boundary layer and can alter convective heat and vapor transfer. Airflow therefore affects plant exchange even when the room's average temperature and humidity remain unchanged.

sections.title: Interpret measurements together
sections.body: Leaf temperature, air temperature, humidity, radiation, and airflow should be interpreted as a system. A single derived number should not replace observation of plant condition and root-zone water supply.

workedExamples: If infrared measurements show leaves several degrees cooler than air, do not assume an air-only VPD chart exactly represents the leaf surface.
If dense interior leaves remain humid despite acceptable room RH, examine local airflow and canopy structure.
Leaves under high irradiance measure 2 °C warmer than air while shaded leaves are near air temperature. A single leaf-temperature offset should not be assumed for the whole canopy.
Two rooms have identical air temperature/RH, but one has stronger airflow. Boundary-layer differences can change leaf heat and vapor exchange even when the room-level VPD matches.
commonMistakes: Assuming leaf temperature always equals air temperature.
Ignoring airflow when comparing rooms with similar temperature and humidity.
Using one leaf-temperature spot measurement as a universal canopy value.
Using one infrared spot as a canopy-wide leaf-temperature value.
Ignoring emissivity, viewing angle or reflective interference when using IR tools.
content.practicalApplication: Measure representative leaf temperatures, note fixture load and airflow, compare them with air temperature and RH, and document whether your VPD method uses air or leaf temperature before interpreting the result.
content.summary: Plant-level vapor-pressure interpretation improves when leaf temperature and boundary-layer conditions are considered alongside room temperature and humidity.

blocks.title: The leaf is the exchange surface
blocks.body: Leaf temperature can differ from air temperature because absorbed radiation, evaporative cooling and convective heat transfer interact at the leaf surface. The thin boundary layer next to the leaf strongly affects that exchange.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.body: Room VPD describes the air; leaf-level exchange depends on leaf temperature, airflow, radiation and plant water status.
